A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 3 \\ 1 & 3 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=-2.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix." :question/worked-solution "Notice that we are given a $3\times 3$ matrix with the following eigenvalues:

- $\lambda =4$ of algebraic multiplicity $2$

- $\lambda =-2$ of algebraic multiplicity $1$

As a result, we have one $1\times 1$ Jordan block ${J}_{1}(-2)$ corresponding to $\lambda =-2.$
However, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda =4:$

- *Case I.* We may get the single $2\times 2$ Jordan block ${J}_{2}(4).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =4$ form the following chain:

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0
$$

- *Case II.* We may get a composition of two $1\times 1$ Jordan blocks, namely ${J}_{1}(4)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(4).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =4$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =4.$

Computing $A-4I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 3 \\ 1 & 3 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 & 3 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 & 3 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+\frac{4}{3}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\text{nullity}(A-4I)=1,$ there will be only one eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =4,$ say, ${v}_{1}.$ So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =4$ form the following chain: 

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0
$$

Therefore, we have *case I*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

$$
{J}_{2}(4)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-2)=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields A=[\begin{aligned}9 & 2 & -2 \\ -6 & 1 & 6 \\ -2 & -2 & 9\end{aligned}]

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=7,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=5.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix." :question/worked-solution "Notice that we are given a $3\times 3$ matrix with the following eigenvalues:

- $\lambda =7$ of algebraic multiplicity $2$

- $\lambda =5$ of algebraic multiplicity $1$

As a result, we have one $1\times 1$ Jordan block ${J}_{1}(5)$ corresponding to $\lambda =5.$
However, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda =7:$

- *Case I.* We may get the single $2\times 2$ Jordan block ${J}_{2}(7).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =7$ form the following chain:

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A-7I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-7I\,}{\to }0
$$

- *Case II.* We may get a composition of two $1\times 1$ Jordan blocks, namely ${J}_{1}(7)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(7).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =7$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A-7I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A-7I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =7.$

Computing $A-7I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-7I & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 2 & -2 \\ -6 & 1 & 6 \\ -2 & -2 & 9\end{aligned}]-7[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & -2 \\ -6 & -6 & 6 \\ -2 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A-7I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & -2 \\ -6 & -6 & 6 \\ -2 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\text{nullity}(A-7I)=2,$ there will be two eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalue $\lambda =7,$ say, ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}.$ So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =7$ form the following chains: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A-7I\,}{\to }0 \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A-7I\,}{\to }0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have *case II*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

$$
{J}_{1}(7)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(7)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(5)=[\begin{aligned}7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields :question/problem "$$
A=[\begin{aligned}9 & 2 & -2 \\ -6 & 1 & 6 \\ -2 & -2 & 9\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=7,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=5.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix." :question/worked-solution "Notice that we are given a $3\times 3$ matrix with the following eigenvalues:

- $\lambda =7$ of algebraic multiplicity $2$

- $\lambda =5$ of algebraic multiplicity $1$

As a result, we have one $1\times 1$ Jordan block ${J}_{1}(5)$ corresponding to $\lambda =5.$
However, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda =7:$

- *Case I.* We may get the single $2\times 2$ Jordan block ${J}_{2}(7).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =7$ form the following chain:

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A-7I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-7I\,}{\to }0
$$

- *Case II.* We may get a composition of two $1\times 1$ Jordan blocks, namely ${J}_{1}(7)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(7).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =7$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A-7I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A-7I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =7.$

Computing $A-7I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-7I & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 2 & -2 \\ -6 & 1 & 6 \\ -2 & -2 & 9\end{aligned}]-7[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & -2 \\ -6 & -6 & 6 \\ -2 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A-7I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & -2 \\ -6 & -6 & 6 \\ -2 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\text{nullity}(A-7I)=2,$ there will be two eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalue $\lambda =7,$ say, ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}.$ So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =7$ form the following chains: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A-7I\,}{\to }0 \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A-7I\,}{\to }0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have *case II*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

$$
{J}_{1}(7)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(7)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(5)=[\begin{aligned}7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields $$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=7,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=5.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix."] ["question-48d72277-36e5-5416-8dca-632269341756" :question/worked-solution "Notice that we are given a $3\times 3$ matrix with the following eigenvalues:

- $\lambda =7$ of algebraic multiplicity $2$

- $\lambda =5$ of algebraic multiplicity $1$

As a result, we have one $1\times 1$ Jordan block ${J}_{1}(5)$ corresponding to $\lambda =5.$
However, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda =7:$

- *Case I.* We may get the single $2\times 2$ Jordan block ${J}_{2}(7).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =7$ form the following chain:

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A-7I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-7I\,}{\to }0
$$

- *Case II.* We may get a composition of two $1\times 1$ Jordan blocks, namely ${J}_{1}(7)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(7).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =7$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A-7I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A-7I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =7.$

Computing $A-7I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-7I & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 2 & -2 \\ -6 & 1 & 6 \\ -2 & -2 & 9\end{aligned}]-7[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & -2 \\ -6 & -6 & 6 \\ -2 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A-7I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & -2 \\ -6 & -6 & 6 \\ -2 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\text{nullity}(A-7I)=2,$ there will be two eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalue $\lambda =7,$ say, ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}.$ So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =7$ form the following chains: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A-7I\,}{\to }0 \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A-7I\,}{\to }0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have *case II*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

$$
{J}_{1}(7)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(7)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(5)=[\begin{aligned}7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks."] ["question-48d72277-36e5-5416-8dca-632269341756" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] 17592186162983 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163277 :tutorial/content "Let's now consider Jordan canonical forms of $3 \times 3$ matrices.

Let $A$ be a $3\times 3$ matrix. The simplest case is when $A$ has three distinct eigenvalues, say $\lambda_1, \lambda_2,$ and  $\lambda_3.$ In this case, $A$ must be diagonalizable. Therefore, the Jordan canonical form of $A$ is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {\lambda }_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

For example, consider the matrix

$$
[\begin{aligned}7 & 1 & -4 \\ 8 & 0 & 2 \\ 4 & -4 & 9\end{aligned}]
$$

This matrix has eigenvalues $\lambda_1=8,$ $\lambda_2=5,$ and $\lambda_3=3.$ Therefore, its Jordan canonical form is

$$
[\begin{aligned}8 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Remember that a Jordan canonical form of a matrix is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks." :tutorial/id #uuid "6659f1d2-f6c2-5a21-815e-c72ad939472d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5464 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "e1f5e4a9-5342-587e-b483-a4199b4f3c0c" :step/math-academy-id 34030 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162989}} {:db/id 17592186162984 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163278 :tutorial/content "Let's now consider the matrix $A,$ given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 6 & 1 \\ 6 & -7 & 9\end{aligned}]
$$

The characteristic equation of $A$ is given by

$$
(\lambda-8)^2(\lambda - 3) = 0.
$$

Therefore, this matrix has only two distinct eigenvalues, namely,

- $\lambda=8$ of algebraic multiplicity $2,$ and

- $\lambda=3$ of algebraic multiplicity $1.$

How can we find its Jordan canonical form?

In this example, we have one $1 \times 1$ Jordan block $J_1(3)$ corresponding to $\lambda=3.$
However, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda=8{:}$

- *Case I.* We may get the single $2 \times 2$ Jordan block $J_2(8).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors $\mathbf v_1$ and $\mathbf v_2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=8$ form the following chain:

$$
\mathbf{v}_2 \xrightarrow{A-8I} \mathbf{v}_1 \xrightarrow{A-8I} \mathbf{0}
$$

- *Case II.* We may get a composition of two $1 \times 1$ Jordan blocks, namely $J_1(8) {\:\oplus\:} J_1(8).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors $\mathbf v_1$ and $\mathbf v_2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=8$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A-8I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A-8I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda=8.$

Computing $A-8I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-8I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 6 & 1 \\ 6 & -7 & 9\end{aligned}]-8[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 & 1 \\ 6 & -7 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A-8I & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 & 1 \\ 6 & -7 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}\leftrightarrow {R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -4 & 3 & 1 \\ 6 & -7 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-6){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & -5 & 5 \\ 0 & 5 & -5\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & -5 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\text{nullity}(A-8I)=1,$ there will be only one eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda=8,$ say, $\mathbf{v}_1.$ So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=8$ form the following chain: 

$$
\mathbf{v}_2 \xrightarrow{A-8I} \mathbf{v}_1 \xrightarrow{A-8I} \mathbf{0}
$$

Therefore, we have *case I*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

$$
[\begin{aligned}8 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

As always, the Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks." :tutorial/id #uuid "630b8bf4-5ce6-5f2a-ac92-8ba6290b80ed" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5465 :tutorial/title "Jordan Canonical Forms of 3x3 Matrices That Have Two Distinct Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "4ca09ce4-ae06-55c7-a22b-c31723893e97" :step/math-academy-id 34031 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162985}} {:db/id 17592186162985 :step/content {:db/id 17592186162064 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161864 :question/id #uuid "79fbc4ff-042e-5454-9fa4-f2582c10a51a" :question/math-academy-id "e-9132"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5a7076c0-fa73-5cb1-9206-2b129dd08be1" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049929}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186162285} {:db/id 17592186162286} {:db/id 17592186247117} {:db/id 17592186247118} {:db/id 17592186247122} {:db/id 17592186367095} {:db/id 17592186397998} {:db/id 17592186398005}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 3x3 Matrix With Two Distinct Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "1d6fb25d-5bc4-5ae7-bf88-ef2a12fcb6cf" :step/math-academy-id 34032 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162986}} {:db/id 17592186162986 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163279 :tutorial/content "Now, suppose we are given  a non-scalar ![](images/59/599d5897394ff1110f6a3bac7053c6836d231de17effad76a1c633d1aed81b33.svg) matrix that has only one eigenvalue ![](images/98/98a445be63a324ba80515c96b7f891797392bdeafb375acb75ce1613f4475d4c.svg) of algebraic multiplicity ![](images/9f/9fc073d1e6ebde82eb949a875e40be00b9196e9b14473ee13fa47a26a98d8450.svg)

Let $A$ be a $3\times 3$ matrix. The simplest case is when $A$ has three distinct eigenvalues, say $\lambda_1, \lambda_2,$ and  $\lambda_3.$ In this case, $A$ must be diagonalizable. Therefore, the Jordan canonical form of $A$ is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {\lambda }_{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

For example, consider the matrix

$$
[\begin{aligned}7 & 1 & -4 \\ 8 & 0 & 2 \\ 4 & -4 & 9\end{aligned}]
$$

This matrix has eigenvalues $\lambda_1=8,$ $\lambda_2=5,$ and $\lambda_3=3.$ Therefore, its Jordan canonical form is

$$
[\begin{aligned}8 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Remember that a Jordan canonical form of a matrix is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks." :tutorial/id #uuid "6659f1d2-f6c2-5a21-815e-c72ad939472d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5464 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "e1f5e4a9-5342-587e-b483-a4199b4f3c0c" :step/math-academy-id 34030 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162989}} {:db/id 17592186163277 :tutorial/content "Let's now consider Jordan canonical forms of $3 \times 3$ matrices.

$$
[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 6 & 1 \\ 6 & -7 & 9\end{aligned}]
$$

The characteristic equation of $A$ is given by

$$
(\lambda-8)^2(\lambda - 3) = 0.
$$

Therefore, this matrix has only two distinct eigenvalues, namely,

- $\lambda=8$ of algebraic multiplicity $2,$ and

- $\lambda=3$ of algebraic multiplicity $1.$

How can we find its Jordan canonical form?

In this example, we have one $1 \times 1$ Jordan block $J_1(3)$ corresponding to $\lambda=3.$
However, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda=8{:}$

- *Case I.* We may get the single $2 \times 2$ Jordan block $J_2(8).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors $\mathbf v_1$ and $\mathbf v_2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=8$ form the following chain:

$$
\mathbf{v}_2 \xrightarrow{A-8I} \mathbf{v}_1 \xrightarrow{A-8I} \mathbf{0}
$$

- *Case II.* We may get a composition of two $1 \times 1$ Jordan blocks, namely $J_1(8) {\:\oplus\:} J_1(8).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors $\mathbf v_1$ and $\mathbf v_2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=8$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A-8I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A-8I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda=8.$

Computing $A-8I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-8I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 6 & 1 \\ 6 & -7 & 9\end{aligned}]-8[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 & 1 \\ 6 & -7 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A-8I & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 & 1 \\ 6 & -7 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}\leftrightarrow {R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -4 & 3 & 1 \\ 6 & -7 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-6){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & -5 & 5 \\ 0 & 5 & -5\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & -5 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\text{nullity}(A-8I)=1,$ there will be only one eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda=8,$ say, $\mathbf{v}_1.$ So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=8$ form the following chain: 

$$
\mathbf{v}_2 \xrightarrow{A-8I} \mathbf{v}_1 \xrightarrow{A-8I} \mathbf{0}
$$

Therefore, we have *case I*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

$$
[\begin{aligned}8 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

As always, the Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks." :tutorial/id #uuid "630b8bf4-5ce6-5f2a-ac92-8ba6290b80ed" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5465 :tutorial/title "Jordan Canonical Forms of 3x3 Matrices That Have Two Distinct Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "4ca09ce4-ae06-55c7-a22b-c31723893e97" :step/math-academy-id 34031 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162985}} {:db/id 17592186163278 :tutorial/content "Let's now consider the matrix $A,$ given by
